entities.name: Query FMO5-like protein
observations: 540 aa protein with calculated molecular mass of 61.2 kDa and theoretical pI 7.03.
Contains a near-full-length FMO-like domain spanning approximately residues 8–532; Pfam i-Evalue 3.3e-204.
Has a predicted C-terminal transmembrane helix around residues 510–530, consistent with membrane anchoring.
Shows 48.8–49.7% identity over 96–97% of its length to reviewed mammalian FMO5 proteins.
Likely binds FAD and NADP(H) as an FMO-family monooxygenase; exact substrate specificity remains uncertain from homology alone.

entities.name: Flavin-containing monooxygenase 5
observations: Reviewed mammalian FMO5 homologs catalyze FAD-dependent NADPH oxidation and Baeyer–Villiger oxidation of ketones to esters.
FMO5 homologs are associated with endoplasmic-reticulum/microsomal membrane localization through a C-terminal transmembrane helix.
Reported biological associations include xenobiotic metabolism, regulation of cholesterol metabolism, and glucose homeostasis; these process-level annotations are organism- and evidence-dependent.

entities.name: FAD/NADP(H) binding
observations: The sequence contains Pfam redox and NAD-binding signatures consistent with an FAD-dependent monooxygenase using NADPH as reducing equivalent.
Candidate reactions include NADPH oxidase activity and Baeyer–Villiger monooxygenation, but exact activity is inferred from homologs rather than directly demonstrated for this sequence.

entities.name: Xenobiotic metabolism
observations: Mammalian FMO5 homolog annotations include xenobiotic metabolic process and oxidation of selected carbonyl-containing compounds.
The query protein may contribute to oxidative metabolism of endogenous or exogenous carbonyl compounds, but substrate range cannot be assigned confidently from sequence alone.

entities.name: Cholesterol and glucose regulation
observations: Reviewed mammalian FMO5 homologs have reported associations with regulation of cholesterol metabolism and glucose homeostasis.
These systems-level biological-process links should be treated as homology-based and organism-specific rather than direct evidence for the query sequence.
